input: what exactly do people mean when they say 'process', is that just the exe file sitting on my hard drive?
expected_output: No. A process is a running program. The program itself is a lifeless thing that just sits on the disk as a bunch of instructions (and maybe some static data), waiting to spring into action; it is the operating system that gets those bytes running.

evidence.quote: The program itself is a lifeless thing: it just sits there on the disk, a bunch of instructions (and maybe some static data), waiting to spring into action.
It is the operating system that takes these bytes and gets them running, transforming the program into something useful.
The definition of a process, informally, is quite simple: it is a running program

input: What does the operating system need to capture to fully describe a running program at a given instant?
expected_output: It needs the program's memory, called its address space, which holds the instructions and the data it reads and writes. It also needs the registers, since many instructions read or update them, and its I/O information, such as a list of the files the process currently has open.

evidence.quote: Thus the memory that the process can address (called its address space) is part of the process.
Also part of the process’s machine state are registers; many instructions explicitly read or update registers and thus clearly they are important to the execution of the process.
Finally, programs often access persistent storage devices too. Such I/O information might include a list of the files the process currently has open.
Instructions lie in memory; the data that the running program reads and writes sits in memory as well.

input: how does my laptop run like 100 things at once when it only has 4 cores
expected_output: The OS runs one process, then stops it and runs another, and so on, which creates the illusion that many virtual CPUs exist when there is really only one physical CPU (or a few). This technique is called time sharing of the CPU. The potential cost is performance, since each process runs more slowly when the CPU has to be shared.

evidence.quote: By running one process, then stopping it and running another, and so forth, the OS can promote the illusion that many virtual CPUs exist when in fact there is only one physical CPU (or a few).

This basic technique, known as time sharing of the CPU, allows users to run as many concurrent processes as they would like; the potential cost is performance, as each will run more slowly if the CPU(s) must be shared.

input: why do operating systems keep the code that does the actual stop-and-start work separate from the code that picks who goes next?
expected_output: The mechanism answers a how question, such as how the OS performs a context switch, while the policy answers a which question, such as which process should run right now. Keeping them separate lets you change policies easily without having to rethink the mechanism, which makes it a form of modularity, a general software design principle.

evidence.quote: You can think of the mechanism as providing the answer to a how question about a system; for example, how does an operating system perform a context switch?
The policy provides the answer to a which question; for example, which process should the operating system run right now?
Separating the two allows one easily to change policies without having to rethink the mechanism and is thus a form of modularity, a general software design principle.

input: what does the os do to a program file before it starts running main?
expected_output: First the OS loads the program's code and any static data from disk into memory, into the address space of the process. It then allocates memory for the run-time stack and initializes it with arguments, filling in the parameters to main() (argc and argv). It may also allocate some memory for the heap, and it does other initialization related to I/O; for example, in UNIX each process by default gets three open file descriptors for standard input, output, and error. Its last task is to start the program running at the entry point, main(), which transfers control of the CPU to the new process.

evidence.quote: The first thing that the OS must do to run a program is to load its code and any static data (e.g., initialized variables) into memory, into the address space of the process.
The OS will also likely initialize the stack with arguments; specifically, it will fill in the parameters to the main() function, i.e., argc and the argv array.
It thus has one last task: to start the program running at the entry point, namely main().
Some memory must be allocated for the program’s run-time stack (or just stack).

By jumping to the main() routine (through a specialized mechanism that we will discuss next chapter), the OS transfers control of the CPU to the newly-created process, and thus the program begins its execution.
The OS may also allocate some memory for the program’s heap.
The OS will also do some other initialization tasks, particularly as related to input/output (I/O).
For example, in UNIX systems, each process by default has three open file descriptors, for standard input, output, and error;

input: how does the os know which sleeping program to wake up when the disk finishes?
expected_output: The OS keeps a process list, tracking processes that are ready along with which process is currently running. It must also track blocked processes in some way, so that when an I/O event completes it can wake the correct process and make it ready to run again.

evidence.quote: To track the state of each process, for example, the OS likely will keep some kind of process list for all processes that are ready, as well as some additional information to track which process is currently running.
The OS must also track, in some way, blocked processes; when an I/O event completes, the OS should make sure to wake the correct process and ready it to run again.

input: whats the difference between a process thats ready and one thats blocked? neither one is actually running
expected_output: A ready process could run right now, but the OS has chosen not to run it at this moment. A blocked process has done some kind of operation, like starting an I/O request, that makes it unable to run until some other event takes place, so it is not ready at all.

evidence.quote: In the ready state, a process is ready to run but for some reason the OS has chosen not to run it at this given moment.
In the blocked state, a process has performed some kind of operation that makes it not ready to run until some other event takes place.

input: how is the way the cpu gets split between programs different from how disk space gets divided up among files?
expected_output: The CPU is time shared: one entity uses it for a little while, then another uses it for a little while, and so on. Disk space is space shared: the resource is divided in space among those who want it, so once a block is assigned to a file it is not likely to be given to another file until the user deletes it.

evidence.quote: By allowing the resource to be used for a little while by one entity, and then a little while by another, and so forth, the resource in question (e.g., the CPU, or a network link) can be shared by many.

space sharing, where a resource is divided (in space) among those who wish to use it. For example, disk space is naturally a space-shared resource, as once a block is assigned to a file, it is not likely to be assigned to another file until the user deletes it.

input: A runs 2 ticks then reads the disk, B needs 6 ticks of cpu. what state is each in when the read starts and ends?
expected_output: Assuming a single CPU: when A starts the disk read it becomes blocked, so B is scheduled and runs. A stays blocked until the I/O completes. At that point A moves from blocked back to ready; whether it runs again immediately or waits for B is a scheduler decision. In the book's matching trace, the OS keeps running the other process, and the process whose I/O finished sits in the ready state until that process is done.

evidence.quote: A common example: when a process initiates an I/O request to a disk, it becomes blocked and thus some other process can use the processor.

Once a process has become blocked (e.g., by initiating an I/O operation), the OS will keep it as such until some event occurs (e.g., I/O completion); at that point, the process moves to the ready state again (and potentially immediately to running again, if the OS so decides).
While Process1 is running, the I/O completes, moving Process0 back to ready.
Second, the system decided not to switch back to Process0 when its I/O completed; it is not clear if this is a good decision or not.

input: child exited with 0 but the parent hasnt checked yet. what state is it in, and what happens once it does?
expected_output: The child sits in a final state where it has exited but has not yet been cleaned up (called the zombie state in UNIX-based systems). This lets the parent examine the return code to see if the child executed successfully (zero usually means success). When the parent makes its final call, e.g. wait(), it waits for the child's completion and indicates to the OS that it can clean up the data structures that referred to the now-extinct process.

evidence.quote: a process could be placed in a final state where it has exited but has not yet been cleaned up (in UNIX-based systems, this is called the zombie state

This final state can be useful as it allows other processes (usually the parent that created the process) to examine the return code of the process and see if the just-finished process executed successfully

When finished, the parent will make one final call (e.g., wait()) to wait for the completion of the child, and to also indicate to the OS that it can clean up any relevant data structures that referred to the now-extinct process.
usually, programs return zero in UNIX-based systems when they have accomplished a task successfully, and non-zero otherwise

input: whats the context field in xv6's struct proc for?
expected_output: The register context holds, for a stopped process, the contents of its registers. When the process is stopped its registers are saved to this memory location, and by restoring them (placing the values back into the actual physical registers) the OS can resume running the process.

evidence.quote: The register context will hold, for a stopped process, the contents of its registers. When a process is stopped, its registers will be saved to this memory location;
by restoring these registers (i.e., placing their values back into the actual physical registers), the OS can resume running the process.

input: pretty sure every os copies the whole program from disk into ram before it executes anything, even the modern ones, right?
expected_output: Not for modern systems. Early or simple operating systems load eagerly, all at once before running the program. Modern OSes load lazily, bringing in pieces of code or data only as they are needed during program execution.

evidence.quote: In early (or simple) operating systems, the loading process is done eagerly, i.e., all at once before running the program; modern OSes perform the process lazily, i.e., by loading pieces of code or data only as they are needed during program execution.

input: If a program is stuck in an infinite loop, is the only option to wait until it quits on its own, since the OS cannot stop a process from the outside?
expected_output: No. Many processes do run and just exit by themselves, but when they don't, the user may wish to kill them. Systems therefore provide an interface to destroy processes forcefully, and an interface to halt a runaway process is quite useful.

evidence.quote: As there is an interface for process creation, systems also provide an interface to destroy processes forcefully.

Of course, many processes will run and just exit by themselves when complete; when they don’t, however, the user may wish to kill them, and thus an interface to halt a runaway process is quite useful.

input: is it really worth the os switching to another program while one waits on the disk?
expected_output: Yes. Running the other process while the first one waits on its I/O improves resource utilization by keeping the CPU busy.

evidence.quote: First, the system had to decide to run Process1 while Process0 issued an I/O; doing so improves resource utilization by keeping the CPU busy.

input: A C program builds a large linked list while it runs, but its dynamic memory area started out tiny. How does the program end up with enough room?
expected_output: In C programs the heap holds dynamically-allocated data that the program explicitly requests with malloc() and releases with free(). The heap is small at first, and as the program runs and requests more memory through the malloc() library API, the OS may get involved and allocate more memory to the process to help satisfy those calls.

evidence.quote: In C programs, the heap is used for explicitly requested dynamically-allocated data; programs request such space by calling malloc() and free it explicitly by calling free().

The heap will be small at first; as the program runs, and requests more memory via the malloc() library API, the OS may get involved and allocate more memory to the process to help satisfy such calls.
